about: IB Mathematics AA HL: the additional higher level (AHL) statements. AA HL = every statement in data/syllabus.json plus every statement here. Codes are the AA guide's own numbers, which never clash with the SL ones (SL 1.1-1.9, AHL 1.10-1.16 and so on). Content is summarised from the guide; ids are permanent and shared with Wasteland Academy's curriculum map. The tagging rules in data/syllabus.json apply; tagWhen is the house rule for when a question part earns the tag, with its boundaries against the SL statements.

statements.title: Counting principles and the binomial theorem for rational indices
statements.content: Counting principles (multiplication and addition rules), permutations and combinations of distinct objects, with arrangements of identical objects and circular arrangements excluded. Extends the binomial theorem to (a + b)^n for rational n, written as a^n(1 + b/a)^n, as an infinite series valid for |b/a| < 1 and used for approximations; proof of the theorem is not required.
statements.tagWhen: Counting selections or arrangements (multiplication and addition principles, nPr, nCr as a count), or expanding (a + b)^n for negative or fractional n and stating where it is valid. A probability found by counting outcomes is 1.10 with 4.5 second; 4.5 alone covers equally likely outcomes that need no counting technique. A binomial expansion with natural n is 1.9, and nCr inside a binomial probability is 4.8.

subtags.name: Count outcomes with the multiplication and addition principles
Count ordered arrangements of distinct objects, with nPr or factorials
Count selections with nCr
Count arrangements or selections with a condition (together, apart, at least one)
Find a probability by counting favourable and total outcomes
Expand (a + b)^n for a negative or fractional n
State or use the interval where a rational-index expansion is valid
Approximate a value or root by substituting into a rational-index expansion

statements.title: Partial fractions
statements.content: Split a proper rational expression into partial fractions when the denominator has at most two distinct linear factors (degree of numerator less than that of the denominator). Repeated factors, irreducible quadratic factors and improper fractions are outside this statement; the main use is rearranging integrands in 5.15.
statements.tagWhen: Splitting a rational expression into partial fractions. When the split is a step in an integral or a differential equation, tag that statement first (5.15 or 5.18) and add 1.11 when the decomposition earns its own marks.

subtags.name: Split a proper fraction over two distinct linear factors
Find the constants by substitution or by comparing coefficients
Rewrite an integrand or a differential equation's fraction as partial fractions

statements.title: Complex numbers in Cartesian form and the complex plane
statements.content: The imaginary unit i with i² = −1, complex numbers in Cartesian form a + bi, and the vocabulary of real part, imaginary part, conjugate, modulus and argument. Includes arithmetic in Cartesian form and representing complex numbers as points or vectors in the complex plane (Argand diagram).
statements.tagWhen: Arithmetic with complex numbers in a + bi form (sums, products, quotients, conjugates, equating real and imaginary parts), modulus or argument as values, or points on an Argand diagram. Converting to polar or Euler form is 1.13.

subtags.name: Add, subtract and multiply complex numbers in a + bi form
Divide complex numbers by multiplying by the conjugate
Equate real and imaginary parts to find unknowns
Find the modulus or argument of a + bi
Represent or read complex numbers as points or vectors on an Argand diagram
Solve a quadratic with complex roots, or one with complex coefficients
Find and use the complex conjugate

statements.title: Modulus-argument and Euler forms of complex numbers
statements.content: Write complex numbers in modulus-argument form r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r cis θ and Euler form re^(iθ), and convert freely between these and Cartesian form. Carry out sums, products and quotients in any form and interpret them geometrically (multiplying moduli and adding arguments as an enlargement and rotation).
statements.tagWhen: Converting between Cartesian, modulus-argument (r cis θ) and Euler (re^(iθ)) forms, or multiplying and dividing in polar form, including reading it as a rotation and enlargement. Powers and roots by De Moivre are 1.14.

subtags.name: Convert a + bi to r cis θ or re^(iθ)
Convert r cis θ or re^(iθ) to a + bi
Multiply or divide in polar or Euler form by combining moduli and arguments
Read multiplication as a rotation and enlargement on the Argand diagram
Use e^(iθ) to express cos θ or sin θ, or sum complex exponentials

statements.title: Conjugate roots, De Moivre's theorem, powers and roots of complex numbers
statements.content: Non-real roots of polynomial equations with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs. De Moivre's theorem (r cis θ)^n = r^n cis nθ, proved by induction for positive integers n and known to hold more widely, is used for powers, nth roots of complex numbers (including roots of unity) and rational exponents.
statements.tagWhen: Powers or nth roots of a complex number by De Moivre's theorem (including roots of unity), or using the conjugate-root theorem for a polynomial with real coefficients. Proving De Moivre by induction is 1.15 with 1.14. Expanding (cis θ)^n to derive a trig identity is 1.14 with the trig statement it produces (3.6 or 3.10).

subtags.name: Raise a complex number to a power with De Moivre's theorem
Find the nth roots of a complex number
Find or use the nth roots of unity, including their sum
Use the conjugate-root theorem to find other roots or the polynomial
Expand (cis θ)^n to derive a multiple-angle or power identity
Use the roots as vertices of a regular polygon, or find areas from them

statements.title: Proof by induction, by contradiction and by counterexample
statements.content: Proof by mathematical induction (for example sums of series, divisibility, derivatives and complex numbers), proof by contradiction (for example irrationality results and the infinitude of primes), and disproof by a counterexample, where the student must show why the example breaks the statement rather than just stating it.
statements.tagWhen: Proof by induction, proof by contradiction, or disproof by counterexample. List the statement being proved second (for example 1.15, 5.12 for an nth-derivative induction). A direct deductive proof is 1.6.

subtags.name: Prove a sum or series result by induction
Prove a divisibility result by induction
Prove an nth-derivative result by induction
Prove an inequality, complex-number or recursive result by induction
Set out the base case, assumption, inductive step and conclusion
Prove a result by contradiction
Disprove a statement with a counterexample that shows why it fails
Conjecture a general formula from calculated cases

statements.title: Systems of linear equations in up to three unknowns
statements.content: Solve systems of up to three linear equations in up to three unknowns, both by algebra (elimination or row reduction) and by technology. Decide whether a system has a unique solution, infinitely many (giving the general solution in terms of a parameter) or none (inconsistent); links to intersecting planes in 3.18.
statements.tagWhen: Solving a system of up to three linear equations (elimination, row reduction or GDC), deciding whether it has a unique solution, none or infinitely many, or giving the general solution with a parameter. Two equations solved as a step inside another topic (such as finding u1 and d) are prior learning. For intersecting planes tag 3.18 first and add 1.16 when solving the system earns marks.

subtags.name: Solve a system of three linear equations with a unique solution
Eliminate or row-reduce a system by algebra
Find the parameter value for which a system has no or infinitely many solutions
Give the general solution of a system in terms of a parameter
Set up a system of linear equations from given conditions

statements.title: Polynomial functions: factor and remainder theorems, sum and product of roots
statements.content: Polynomial functions of any degree: their graphs, zeros, roots and factors; the factor and remainder theorems; and the sum (−aₙ₋₁/aₙ) and product ((−1)ⁿa₀/aₙ) of the roots of a polynomial equation, including equations with complex roots. Only the sum and the product of the roots are listed, not sums of pairwise products.
statements.tagWhen: Factor or remainder theorem, polynomial division, finding unknown coefficients from a factor or remainder, the sum or product of the roots, or the graph and zeros of a polynomial of degree 3 or more. Solving or factorising a quadratic is 2.7, including a quadratic factor left after dividing a cubic, unless the cubic work itself earns marks.

subtags.name: Use the factor theorem to show a factor or find a coefficient
Use the remainder theorem to find a remainder or a coefficient
Divide a polynomial by a linear or quadratic factor
Factorise a cubic or quartic and find all its roots
Use the sum or product of the roots of a polynomial
Sketch or read the graph, zeros and multiplicities of a polynomial
Write a polynomial from its roots or graph features
Prove a general property of the roots of a polynomial

statements.title: Rational functions with a quadratic numerator or denominator
statements.content: Rational functions with a linear numerator over a quadratic denominator, and with a quadratic numerator over a linear denominator, with the reciprocal function as a special case. Sketches must show every asymptote (vertical, horizontal and oblique) and all axis intercepts.
statements.tagWhen: Rational functions with a quadratic numerator or denominator: their vertical, horizontal or oblique asymptotes, intercepts and sketches. Linear over linear functions are 2.8.

subtags.name: Find vertical asymptotes from a quadratic denominator
Find a horizontal asymptote of a rational function
Find an oblique asymptote by division
Find the axis intercepts of a rational function
Sketch a rational function with its asymptotes and intercepts
Find the range or excluded values of a rational function

statements.title: Odd and even functions, inverses with a restricted domain, self-inverse functions
statements.content: Odd functions (f(−x) = −f(x)) and even functions (f(−x) = f(x)), including periodic ones such as sin, cos and tan; finding an inverse function, restricting the domain where needed so that one exists; and self-inverse functions, where f⁻¹ = f.
statements.tagWhen: Testing or using odd and even symmetry, finding an inverse that needs a restricted domain (such as the largest domain on which f^-1 exists), or self-inverse functions. An inverse of a one-to-one function with no domain question is 2.5.

subtags.name: Show or decide whether a function is odd, even or neither
Use odd or even symmetry to find values, integrals or graphs
Find the largest domain on which an inverse exists
Find an inverse function on a restricted domain, with its domain and range
Show that a function is self-inverse or use that property

statements.title: Solving inequalities g(x) ≥ f(x) graphically and analytically
statements.content: Solving inequalities of the form g(x) ≥ f(x) both from graphs and analytically. Algebraic or graphical methods are expected for simple polynomials up to degree 3; technology is used for these and for other functions.
statements.tagWhen: Solving an inequality g(x) ≥ f(x), by algebra or a graph for polynomials up to degree 3 or with the GDC otherwise. A quadratic inequality on its own is 2.7 and a modulus inequality is 2.16. Finding where f'(x) > 0 is 5.2; add 2.15 only when solving the inequality earns separate marks.

subtags.name: Solve a polynomial inequality by factorising and a sign diagram
Solve g(x) ≥ f(x) from a graph or with the GDC
Solve an inequality with a rational expression without multiplying by an unknown sign

statements.title: Graphs of |f(x)|, f(|x|), 1/f(x), f(ax + b) and [f(x)]²; modulus equations and inequalities
statements.content: Graphs of y = |f(x)|, y = f(|x|), y = 1/f(x), y = f(ax + b) and y = [f(x)]² drawn from the graph of y = f(x); and solving equations and inequalities that involve the modulus, algebraically for simple cases and with technology otherwise.
statements.tagWhen: Sketching y = |f(x)|, f(|x|), 1/f(x), f(ax + b) or [f(x)]^2 from the graph of y = f(x), or solving an equation or inequality that involves a modulus. Other translations, stretches and reflections are 2.11.

subtags.name: Sketch y = |f(x)| from the graph of y = f(x)
Sketch y = f(|x|) from the graph of y = f(x)
Sketch y = 1/f(x) from the graph of y = f(x)
Sketch y = [f(x)]² or y = f(ax + b) from the graph of y = f(x)
Solve an equation involving a modulus
Solve an inequality involving a modulus

statements.title: Reciprocal trigonometric ratios, Pythagorean identities and inverse trigonometric functions
statements.content: Defines sec θ, cosec θ and cot θ as the reciprocals of cos θ, sin θ and tan θ, and adds the Pythagorean identities 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ. Covers arcsin x, arccos x and arctan x as functions: their restricted domains, principal-value ranges and graphs.
statements.tagWhen: sec, cosec and cot, the identities 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ, or arcsin, arccos and arctan as functions (domain, range, graph, exact values). sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 and the sin and cos double angles are 3.6. Differentiating or integrating inverse trig functions is 5.15.

subtags.name: Use sec, cosec and cot, including exact values
Use 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ or 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ
Solve an equation in sec, cosec or cot
Find exact values of arcsin, arccos or arctan
Use the domain, range or graph of an inverse trig function
Express an angle or variable using arcsin, arccos or arctan

statements.title: Compound angle identities
statements.content: Compound angle identities for sin(A ± B), cos(A ± B) and tan(A ± B), and the double angle identity for tan. Includes deriving the double angle identities from the compound ones, with a link to De Moivre's theorem.
statements.tagWhen: Using a compound angle identity (sin, cos or tan of A ± B) or the double angle identity for tan. The sin 2θ and cos 2θ identities alone are 3.6.

subtags.name: Expand or use sin, cos or tan of A ± B
Use the double angle identity for tan
Find an exact value with a compound angle identity
Prove an identity using compound angle formulae
Solve an equation that needs a compound angle identity

statements.title: Relationships between trigonometric functions and the symmetry of their graphs
statements.content: Relationships between the trigonometric functions shown by the symmetries of their graphs and the unit circle, such as sin(π − θ) = sin θ, cos(π − θ) = −cos θ and tan(π − θ) = −tan θ. Links to odd and even functions and to compound angles.
statements.tagWhen: Using a symmetry relation such as sin(π − θ) = sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ or tan(π + θ) = tan θ to simplify an expression or find values. Exact values and quadrant signs alone are 3.5.

subtags.name: Use sin(π − θ), cos(−θ), tan(π + θ) and similar relations
Simplify a trigonometric expression using symmetry of the graphs
Find values of one trig function from another using symmetry

statements.title: Vectors: concepts, components and algebra
statements.content: Vectors as directed line segments, written in column form or with base vectors i, j, k. Position and displacement vectors (AB = b − a), sums, differences, scalar multiples, the zero vector, parallel vectors, magnitude, unit vectors and the distance between points, treated both algebraically and geometrically, plus proofs of geometric properties with vectors.
statements.tagWhen: Vector algebra and geometry: position and displacement vectors (AB = b − a), sums and scalar multiples, magnitude, unit vectors, parallel vectors, the distance between points as a vector magnitude, or a geometric proof with vectors. Distances, midpoints and angles in a 3D solid found without vectors are 3.1.

subtags.name: Find a displacement vector AB = b − a or a position vector
Add, subtract and scale vectors, or find an unknown point from a vector relation
Find a magnitude, unit vector or a vector of given length
Use or show that two vectors are parallel or points are collinear
Find a distance between points as a vector magnitude
Prove a geometric result with vectors

statements.title: The scalar product and the angle between vectors
statements.content: The scalar (dot) product, both in components and as v · w = |v||w| cos θ, and its algebraic properties. Using it to find the angle between vectors and to test for perpendicular vectors (v · w = 0) and parallel vectors (|v · w| = |v||w|).
statements.tagWhen: The scalar product: computing v · w, the angle between two vectors, or testing for perpendicular vectors. An angle in a 3D solid found by trigonometry is 3.1 (with 3.2). The angle between two lines is 3.14 with 3.13; between a line and a plane or two planes it is 3.18.

subtags.name: Compute a scalar product
Find the angle between two vectors
Use v · w = 0 to test or impose perpendicularity
Expand or manipulate scalar products algebraically, such as |a + b|²

statements.title: Vector equation of a line in two and three dimensions
statements.content: The vector equation of a line r = a + λb in 2D and 3D, the meaning of the position vector a and direction vector b, and its parametric and Cartesian forms. The angle between two lines from their direction vectors, and simple kinematics with λ as time, b as velocity and |b| as speed.
statements.tagWhen: Writing or using the vector, parametric or Cartesian equation of a line, checking whether a point is on a line, the angle between two lines (add 3.13 when the scalar product earns marks), or kinematics with r = a + tv (position, velocity vector, speed). Kinematics by calculus is 5.9.

subtags.name: Write the vector, parametric or Cartesian equation of a line
Check whether a point lies on a line or find a point with a given condition
Convert between vector, parametric and Cartesian forms of a line
Find the angle between two lines from their direction vectors
Find the closest point on a line to a point, or the shortest distance
Use r = a + tv for position, velocity, speed or meeting objects

statements.title: Coincident, parallel, intersecting and skew lines
statements.content: Deciding whether two lines are coincident, parallel, intersecting or skew (non-parallel and non-intersecting, possible only in 3D), and finding the point of intersection when there is one.
statements.tagWhen: Deciding whether two lines are coincident, parallel, intersecting or skew, or finding where two lines meet. A line meeting a plane is 3.18.

subtags.name: Decide whether two lines are parallel, intersecting, skew or coincident
Find where two lines meet
Find the shortest distance between two skew or parallel lines

statements.title: The vector product
statements.content: The vector (cross) product in components and as v × w = |v||w| sin θ n with n given by the right-hand rule, and its properties: anticommutative, distributive, v × v = 0, and zero for non-zero vectors exactly when they are parallel. Using |v × w| for the area of a parallelogram or triangle.
statements.tagWhen: Computing a vector product, or using |v × w| for the area of a triangle or parallelogram. When the vector product is only a step to a plane's normal, tag 3.17 first and add 3.16 if it earns marks.

subtags.name: Compute a vector product
Find an area with |v × w|
Find a vector perpendicular to two given vectors
Use the properties of the vector product algebraically

statements.title: Vector and Cartesian equations of a plane
statements.content: Equations of a plane in vector form r = a + λb + μc (b, c non-parallel vectors in the plane), scalar product form r · n = a · n with normal n, and Cartesian form ax + by + cz = d.
statements.tagWhen: Writing or using the equation of a plane in vector, scalar product or Cartesian form, or checking whether a point lies in a plane.

subtags.name: Write the equation of a plane in vector, scalar product or Cartesian form
Find a plane's normal from three points or two directions
Check whether a point lies in a plane or find a constant
Convert between vector and Cartesian forms of a plane

statements.title: Intersections and angles between lines and planes
statements.content: Intersections of a line with a plane, of two planes and of three planes, found by solving equations and interpreted geometrically (a point, a line, a plane, or no intersection), linking to systems of linear equations. The angle between a line and a plane and between two planes.
statements.tagWhen: Where a line meets a plane, the intersection of two or three planes and what it looks like geometrically, or the angle between a line and a plane or between two planes, found with vectors. Add 1.16 when solving the linear system earns marks. The angle between a line and a plane in a 3D solid found by trigonometry is 3.1.

subtags.name: Find where a line meets a plane
Find the line of intersection of two planes
Find or describe the intersection of three planes
Find the angle between a line and a plane with vectors
Find the angle between two planes
Find the distance from a point to a plane, or a reflection in a plane

statements.title: Bayes' theorem
statements.content: Using Bayes' theorem to reverse a conditional probability, with at most three events in the partition, for example in medical testing where a test result is used to update the chance of having a disease. Builds on conditional probability and independence from SL.
statements.tagWhen: Bayes' theorem: reversing a conditional probability, finding P(A | B) from P(B | A), usually from a tree diagram. A forward conditional probability read from a diagram is 4.6, with 4.11 when the formula is used.

subtags.name: Reverse a conditional probability from a tree diagram
Use Bayes' theorem with two or three events
Find P(B) by summing over a partition first

statements.title: Discrete and continuous random variables: pdfs, mean, variance, median and mode
statements.content: Variance of discrete random variables, and continuous random variables defined by probability density functions (including piecewise ones) that integrate to 1. Covers the mode and median of a continuous variable, E(X), E(X²), Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² and standard deviation for both types, fair games, and the effect of the linear transformation aX + b.
statements.tagWhen: Continuous random variables (a pdf integrating to 1, P(a < X < b) by integration, mean, variance, median, mode), the variance of a discrete random variable, E(X²), or the mean and variance of aX + b. A discrete distribution table, sum of probabilities = 1, E(X) or a fair game is 4.7; add 4.14 for the variance, E(X²) or a linear transformation. Integrating a pdf is part of 4.14; add a calculus statement only when the technique (such as 5.16) earns its own marks.

subtags.name: Find a constant so that a pdf integrates to 1
Find P(a < X < b) by integrating a pdf
Find the mean of a continuous random variable
Find the variance or E(X²) of a continuous random variable
Find the median or mode of a continuous random variable
Find the variance or E(X²) of a discrete random variable
Use E(aX + b) and Var(aX + b)

statements.title: Continuity, differentiability, limits and differentiation from first principles
statements.content: An informal sense of continuity and differentiability at a point (never tested formally), limits as convergence or divergence, and the derivative defined from first principles as the limit of (f(x + h) − f(x))/h, used for polynomials only. Higher derivatives with the notations dⁿy/dxⁿ and f⁽ⁿ⁾(x), including nth-derivative patterns proved by induction.
statements.tagWhen: Differentiation from first principles, continuity or differentiability at a point (such as where two pieces of a function join), the limit of a sequence or function found by reasoning about convergence, or higher derivatives f^(n)(x) and nth-derivative patterns (with 1.15 when proved by induction). The derivative read as a rate or gradient is 5.1.

subtags.name: Differentiate from first principles
Show or impose continuity at a point
Show or impose differentiability where two pieces join
Find a limit of a function or sequence by reasoning about its behaviour
Find higher derivatives or an nth-derivative pattern

statements.title: Limits by l'Hôpital's rule or Maclaurin series
statements.content: Limits of quotients f(x)/g(x) as x → a or x → ∞ that give the indeterminate forms 0/0 or ∞/∞, found with l'Hôpital's rule (applied more than once if needed) or by Maclaurin series. Includes the standard result sin θ/θ → 1 as θ → 0 and links to horizontal asymptotes.
statements.tagWhen: A limit of the form 0/0 or ∞/∞ found with l'Hôpital's rule (once or repeatedly) or with a Maclaurin series. Add 5.19 when the series has to be built, not just quoted.

subtags.name: Find a 0/0 or ∞/∞ limit with l'Hôpital's rule
Apply l'Hôpital's rule more than once
Find a limit by substituting Maclaurin series
Use sin θ/θ → 1 or a similar standard limit
Use the need for a 0/0 form to find an unknown constant

statements.title: Implicit differentiation, related rates of change and optimisation
statements.content: Implicit differentiation of relations in x and y, related rates of change linked by the chain rule, and optimisation problems, including cases where the best value is at an endpoint of the domain rather than at a stationary point.
statements.tagWhen: Implicit differentiation (dy/dx of a relation in x and y; add 5.4 for a tangent or normal), related rates of change linked by the chain rule (such as dV/dt from dr/dt), or optimisation where an endpoint must be checked. A stationary-point optimisation with no related rates, implicit relation or endpoint argument is 5.8.

subtags.name: Find dy/dx by implicit differentiation
Find a tangent, normal or stationary point on an implicit curve
Link rates of change with the chain rule
Optimise where an endpoint or domain restriction must be checked
Find d²y/dx² implicitly

statements.title: Further standard derivatives and integrals
statements.content: Derivatives of tan x, sec x, cosec x, cot x, aˣ, logₐ x, arcsin x, arccos x and arctan x, the matching indefinite integrals (read as a family of curves), and the same results for composites with a linear function. Partial fractions (up to two distinct linear factors) are used to rearrange integrands.
statements.tagWhen: Differentiating or integrating tan, sec, cosec, cot, a^x, log_a x, arcsin, arccos or arctan, including their composites with chain, product or quotient rules, or integrals that become standard after partial fractions (add 1.11). Do not also tag 5.6 or 5.10 for the same derivative or integral.

subtags.name: Differentiate tan, sec, cosec or cot
Differentiate a^x or log_a x
Differentiate arcsin, arccos or arctan
Integrate using the further standard integrals, including inverse trig results
Integrate after splitting into partial fractions
Differentiate or integrate these functions composed with ax + b

statements.title: Integration by substitution and by parts
statements.content: Integration by substitution beyond the reverse chain rule (the substitution is given unless the integral has the form ∫ k g′(x) f(g(x)) dx), with changed limits for definite integrals. Integration by parts, including repeated use and the cyclic case such as ∫ eˣ sin x dx.
statements.tagWhen: Integration by substitution beyond the reverse chain rule (a given substitution such as u = √x or x = sin θ, often with changed limits) or integration by parts, including repeated and cyclic cases. An integral of the form ∫ k g'(x) f(g(x)) dx, by inspection or by substitution, is 5.10.

subtags.name: Integrate with a given substitution
Change the limits of a definite integral under a substitution
Integrate by parts once
Integrate by parts more than once
Solve a cyclic integration by parts such as ∫ eˣ sin x dx
Derive or use a reduction formula by parts

statements.title: Areas against the y-axis and volumes of revolution
statements.content: Areas between a curve and the y-axis over a y-interval, found by integrating x with respect to y. Volumes of solids formed by rotating a region through 2π about the x-axis (V = π∫ y² dx) or the y-axis (V = π∫ x² dy), including regions between two curves and design contexts.
statements.tagWhen: The area between a curve and the y-axis (integrating with respect to y), or a volume of revolution about the x-axis or y-axis. Areas against the x-axis or between two curves in x are 5.5 or 5.11.

subtags.name: Find an area against the y-axis by integrating with respect to y
Find a volume of revolution about the x-axis
Find a volume of revolution about the y-axis
Find a volume of revolution of a region between two curves
Rewrite a curve as x in terms of y to integrate

statements.title: First-order differential equations
statements.content: First-order differential equations: numerical solution of dy/dx = f(x, y) by Euler's method with constant step h; exact solution of separable equations (including the logistic equation, using partial fractions), homogeneous equations dy/dx = f(y/x) via y = vx, and linear equations y′ + P(x)y = Q(x) via an integrating factor. Contexts include cooling, population growth and radioactive decay.
statements.tagWhen: Setting up or solving a first-order differential equation: Euler's method, separation of variables, the substitution y = vx for a homogeneous equation, or an integrating factor. dy/dx = f(x) solved by direct integration is 5.5 or 5.10. Add 1.11 when partial fractions earn marks, and 5.16 when substitution or parts is needed inside.

subtags.name: Approximate a solution with Euler's method

Solve a linear equation with an integrating factor
Use an initial condition to find a particular solution
Set up a differential equation from a context
Interpret a solution or its long-run behaviour in context
Transform a differential equation with a given substitution

statements.title: Maclaurin series
statements.content: Maclaurin series for eˣ, sin x, cos x, ln(1 + x) and (1 + x)ᵖ with p rational, and new series built from these by substitution, multiplication, differentiation and integration. Series can also be developed from a differential equation by repeated differentiation.
statements.tagWhen: Building or using a Maclaurin series: from the standard series, by substitution, multiplication, differentiation or integration, or from a differential equation by repeated differentiation, including approximations from the series. A limit found by series is 5.13 with 5.19. The series for (1 + x)^p found by the binomial theorem is 1.10; derived by differentiating, it is 5.19.

subtags.name: Use the standard Maclaurin series for eˣ, sin x, cos x, ln(1 + x) or (1 + x)^p

Multiply series together
